name: Monads
plain_explanation: Leibniz believed the universe is made up of an infinite number of simple, non-physical, soul-like units called monads, rather than physical matter; even what looks like solid matter is really a colony of these mind-like units.
precise_definition: Simple, unextended substances, each essentially a soul with perceptions of varying clarity, that make up all of reality; Leibniz denied that extension could be an attribute of a true substance because extension implies plurality, so genuine substances must be unextended and therefore mental.
why_it_mattered: It is Leibniz's solution to the problem of substance: rather than three substances (Descartes) or one (Spinoza), he posits infinitely many, each a distinct point of view on the universe.
historical_origin: Developed in the Monadology and the Principles of Nature and of Grace, written for royal patrons.
examples: A human body is composed entirely of monads, each a soul, with one 'dominant monad' constituting what we call the person's mind.
No two monads are exactly alike (the principle of the identity of indiscernibles).
objections: Russell says the doctrine that monads are 'windowless' creates the puzzle of how any monad could know there are others at all - what looks like mirroring the universe could simply be a private dream.
Leibniz is 'guilty of a special inconsistency' in combining subject-predicate logic (which implies monism) with a pluralism of many monads.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says Leibniz's two kinds of space - subjective (within each monad's perception) and objective (the arrangement of viewpoints) - remain useful for relating perception to physics.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The 'dominant monad' explains, for Leibniz, what common sense calls the will's control over the body.
